extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students/scholars of literature and dramaturgy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic and dramatic works (especially tragedy): which means, objects, and manners of imitation to use; the essential parts of tragedy; and how plot, character, diction, thought, song, and spectacle should be organized and weighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation — means (rhythm, melody, metre, language)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts differ with respect to the means by which they imitate: rhythm, melody (song), and metre, or language alone (prose or verse); some arts employ all together, others only one (e.g., dancing uses rhythm alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate medium of imitation for the artform: include rhythm/melody where musical elements are needed; recognize that verse may combine different metres or use a single kind. Example: pipe/dance use rhythm without harmony; dithyrambic and nomic poetry employ rhythm, melody and metre together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation — choice of character-type (better, worse, as they are)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects imitated are persons acting; they must be represented as either better than in real life, worse, or as they are — moral quality (goodness/badness) distinguishes these types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to portray elevated (noble) types, base/mean types, or realistic types — this choice helps determine the genre (e.g., Tragedy tends to present men as better than they are; Comedy as worse). Examples: Homer depicts men nobler; others (e.g., Nicochares) depict men worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation — narration vs dramatic enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration (telling) — either adopting another personality or speaking in his own person — or by making actors live and move before the audience (dramatic enactment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether the work will present action through enacted scenes or through narrated report; the dramatic (enacted) manner is what gives rise to 'drama' as a distinct form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy — serious, complete action of certain magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is mimesis (imitation) of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; it should be in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; presented as action (not narrative); and effect a catharsis of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the action is unified and significant (not trivial), the language includes artistic ornament (meter, melody), and the play aims to arouse and purify pity and fear. Avoid fragmentary or trivial plots; tragedy should aim at a single, cohesive serious action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos) — the chief element; unity, causality, beginning-middle-end
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the structure/arrangement of incidents and is the most important part of tragedy — it must be a complete whole (beginning, middle, end), of appropriate magnitude, and constituted by linked causal incidents (not a mere collection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a single unified action where events follow by necessity or probability; avoid disconnected episodic multiplicity. The plot should be memorable and of such length that the course of events (e.g., a change from good fortune to bad) can be apprehended. Vital plot devices include peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition), which provide emotional interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (êthos) — reveals moral purpose and supports action
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that quality by which we ascribe certain moral dispositions or choices to agents; it determines what sorts of actions characters are likely to perform, but is subsidiary to plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters consistent and apt to the actions required by the plot; mere finely crafted speeches and ethical portraiture cannot substitute for a strong plot. Characters should reveal pre dispositions by choices they make in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — reasoning and themes expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of stating, proving, or expressing general truths and the possible/pertinent in circumstances (the intellectual content of speeches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to make characters argue convincingly, express beliefs or demonstrable positions, and to articulate the play's themes — this is the rhetorical/political dimension of dramatic dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — expression and metrical arrangement of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction denotes the expression of meaning in words; its essence includes metrical arrangement in verse and functioning similarly in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft phrasing and metrical arrangement to suit the form and to express meaning effectively. Note that excellent diction alone cannot produce the essential tragic effect if plot is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song / Melody (melopoiia) — chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (the musical element) is the greatest of the pleasures among the embellishments of a tragedy and is central to its artistic appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate musical elements where parts of the play call for them (choral odes, lyrical sections) to enhance emotional impact; treat song as a central artistic component, distinct from mere diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Visuals (opsis) — scenic equipment and stage effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle refers to the visual elements (scenery, stagecraft) of a production; it is a part of tragedy but the least artistic and least connected with poetic theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that spectacle has strong emotional attraction but depends more on stage-craft than on the poet's art; do not rely on spectacle to substitute for a well-constructed plot and strong poetic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of plot over rhetoric, character, and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (structure of incidents) is the primary determinant of a tragedy's quality; character, diction, and thought, while important, are subordinate to and serve the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing drama, prioritize the integrity and unity of the plot: a play with an effective plot will achieve tragic effects better than one with only fine speeches or character sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Length appropriate to perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must have a magnitude suitable to perception: not so short as to be trivial nor so long as to exceed the audience's capacity to apprehend it; tragedy aims (ideally) at a single revolution of the sun, while epic has no time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a length that allows the single unified action to unfold clearly and memorably within performance constraints; avoid extremes (too brief to be seen as full, or so long that the audience cannot take it in at once).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of metre to subject and mode (measure selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different metres suit different subjects and modes: iambic is colloquial and fit for lampoons/iambic satire; hexameter suits epic (narrative) verse; trochaic tetrameter was used in earlier satyric/choral forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre that aligns with genre and rhetorical tone: e.g., iambic for colloquial/lampooning effects, hexameter for epic narrative. Meter choice affects voice and audience perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Comedy — imitation of lower types; the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower/more base type; the ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly — a defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive (a harmless deformity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose comedy by portraying lesser characters and exploiting the ludicrous (harmless faults); avoid making the comic simply cruel or painful — the ludicrous should not cause real suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of poetry — human instincts (imitation and harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from two natural instincts: the instinct to imitate (present from childhood and fundamental to learning) and the instinct for harmony and rhythm (pleasure in rhythm/measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating poetry, appeal to innate mimetic and rhythmic instincts — use likeness, rhythm, and harmony to engage audiences and facilitate learning/pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of means across parts (some parts in verse, others in song)
rubrics_metrics.description: The several kinds of artistic means are found in separate parts of the play: some parts are rendered through verse alone, others with the aid of song (choral sections), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the play so that different sections use the medium most appropriate to their function (e.g., lyrical choral odes for lyric moments, metrical diction for speech); avoid misplacing modes such that function and medium conflict.
